title: Addition Within 10 for Grade 1: Master Sums to Ten First + Free Quiz
meta_title: Addition Within 10 Grade 1: Bonds to Ten Guide
meta_desc: Master addition within 10 in Grade 1 before crossing ten. The full set of number bonds to 10, ten-frame tips, fluency games and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Before a child can add 8 + 5, they need every sum up to 10 to feel automatic. Here is why the 0–10 range is the real foundation, the complete set of bonds to ten, and how to make them stick.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Put 3 + 4 in front of a Grade 1 child and watch what happens. If they still count ‘one, two, three… four, five, six, seven’ from the very start, they are not ready for 8 + 5 yet, no matter what the textbook schedule says. Addition within 10 for Grade 1 is the range where fluency is actually built — every sum that stays at or below ten — and rushing past it to cross the ten-line is the single most common mistake I see parents make.

Here is the case for slowing down. There are only 66 addition facts with a sum of 10 or less, and a good chunk of them (adding 0, adding 1) are almost free. That is a small, finite set a six-year-old can genuinely own. Once these are automatic, the harder work of crossing ten leans on them completely — you cannot make ten out of 8 + 5 if you do not instantly know that 8 needs 2. So the sums to ten are not a warm-up. They are the whole foundation.

Why the 0–10 range comes first

Fingers are the giveaway. A child can count 4 + 3 on fingers and land on 7, but the moment a sum passes ten they run out of fingers and the method collapses. If we push crossing-ten work before the within-ten facts are solid, the child has no fallback and quietly decides maths is confusing. Keeping the range at 10 or below for a good few weeks lets them succeed every single time, and success is what makes a six-year-old want to keep going.

The NCERT-aligned Grade 1 sequence agrees: numbers to 9, then the number 10, then addition within 10, and only later addition up to 20. The order is not an accident. Ten is the hinge our whole number system turns on, so a child who truly knows ten — every way to build it, every way to break it — has the key to place value waiting for them.

The complete set of number bonds to 10

A number bond is just a pair of numbers that join to make a total. The bonds to ten are the ones worth memorising cold, because they show up everywhere for years. There are only six pairs to learn (order aside), and most children can hold all of them within a fortnight of daily practice.

First partSecond partBond
0100 + 10 = 10
191 + 9 = 10
282 + 8 = 10
373 + 7 = 10
464 + 6 = 10
555 + 5 = 10

Notice the pattern: as the first part climbs 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the second part falls 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5. Children love spotting this — it turns six facts into one idea. And every bond is really a small family: because order does not matter, 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 both make ten, which halves what there is to remember.

Use a ten-frame, not flashcards

A ten-frame is two rows of five squares — ten boxes in all. It is the best five-rupee teaching tool I know; you can draw one on the back of an old bill. Put down some counters (rajma beans, buttons, coins) and the child sees the sum instead of just hearing it.

  • Place 6 beans and ask ‘how many more to fill the frame?’ The empty boxes answer 4 — that is the bond 6 + 4 = 10, seen with the eyes.
  • Fill the top row fully (5) and add 2 below: the child reads 5 + 2 = 7 without counting from one, because five is already a familiar chunk.
  • Ask them to make 8 two different ways — say 5 and 3, then 4 and 4. This quietly teaches that a number has many bonds, not one.

The frame matters because it builds ‘subitising’ — recognising a small quantity at a glance without counting. A child who sees five as one chunk, not five separate ones, is already halfway to fluency.

The easy wins hiding in the range

Two rules clear away a surprising number of questions with almost no effort. Adding zero changes nothing: 7 + 0 is just 7. Adding one gives the next counting number: 6 + 1 is 7, the number that comes straight after. Teach these two explicitly. They remove a whole column from any within-ten worksheet and, as a bonus, reinforce the order of numbers — the seed of the number line that subtraction will need later.

Fluency games that fit in ten minutes

Fluency is not drilling until a child cries. It is short, cheerful, and frequent. A few that have worked for families I know:

  • Make-ten snap. Say a number; the child shouts its partner to ten. You say 3, they say 7. Aim for under two seconds, no counting.
  • Dice-and-fingers. Roll one die, add fingers to reach a target under ten. Roll a 4, target 9, they hold up 5.
  • Rangoli dots. Draw two small groups of dots (say 3 and 5), ask for the total. Real objects and patterns beat abstract symbols at this age.

One honest caveat: do not chase speed before understanding. A child who works out 4 + 5 by thinking ‘4 and 4 is 8, one more is 9’ is in a stronger place than one who has rote-memorised it but freezes when the numbers change. Speed follows sound thinking on its own — never the other way round.

How to know they are ready to cross ten

The signal is simple. When your child can answer any sum up to 10 in a couple of seconds, without fingers and without that tell-tale pause, they have the foundation. Now the making-ten strategy for sums like 8 + 5 will feel like a natural next step rather than a wall. Get the within-ten range genuinely automatic first, and everything after it — crossing ten, subtraction, place value — comes far more easily.

Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Addition Within 10 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on sums within ten, number bonds to 10 and missing parts. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Start from the bigger number, 4, and count on three: 5, 6, 7.
3 and 7 fill a ten-frame exactly. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.
This is a double and also a bond to ten. Double 5 is 10.
6 needs 4 more to fill the ten-frame, so the bond is 6 + 4 = 10.
Start from the bigger number, 6, and count on two: 7, 8.
3 and 7 are a bond to ten, so the missing part is 7.

questions.q: A basket has 4 mangoes and 5 more are added. How many now?
questions.explanation: 4 + 5 stays within ten. Think double 4 is 8, one more makes 9.

faq.q: Why teach addition within 10 before sums up to 20?
faq.a: Because every harder strategy leans on it. To add 8 + 5 by making ten, a child must instantly know that 8 needs 2 — a bond to ten. If the within-ten facts are shaky, crossing ten has nothing to stand on.

faq.q: What are the number bonds to 10?
faq.a: The pairs that join to make ten: 0 and 10, 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, and 5 and 5. Six pairs in all — learn these cold and much of primary arithmetic gets easier for years.

faq.q: How long should a child spend on sums within 10?
faq.a: As long as it takes for the answers to come in a couple of seconds without fingers — usually a few weeks of ten-minute sessions. There is no prize for moving on early; a solid foundation saves months later.

faq.q: Is it fine if my child still uses fingers for these sums?
faq.a: At the start, yes — fingers make the maths concrete. The aim is to give better tools, like a ten-frame and bonds to ten, so the child chooses to leave fingers behind rather than being told to.
